prompt: Why does the lesson treat the administrator's path to a server more carefully than any other?

choices.text: Because SSH is older than the other protocols the course protects
choices.why: Age is not the argument; where the path ends is.

choices.text: Because administrators make more mistakes than other users
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so; the value of the path is the point.

choices.text: Because it carries more traffic than the portal does
choices.why: It carries little traffic; it carries a lot of power.

choices.text: It ends at root on the server
choices.why: Right, and from there at whatever that server trusts.

prompt: Before the lesson, a phishing link runs on desk. Why does that matter to web?

choices.text: desk holds a key web accepts, so desk is a way to web
choices.why: Right. Every machine with the key was a door.

choices.text: desk and web share a disk
choices.why: They are separate containers with separate disks.

choices.text: Phishing spreads to every machine on the same segment on its own
choices.why: It needs a path; the shared key is the path.

choices.text: web trusts desk's address for its database
choices.why: No such trust exists here; SSH does.

prompt: What turns a jump server from a convenience into a control?

choices.text: A faster connection than the direct path
choices.why: Speed makes people use it on good days; it does not stop the other days.

choices.text: The servers refuse administration from anywhere else
choices.why: Right. Otherwise people go round it the day it matters.

choices.text: Installing every administration tool the team uses on it
choices.why: The opposite: it should do nothing else.

choices.text: Giving each administrator their own account on it
choices.why: Useful for the log, and still optional while other paths exist.

prompt: With ProxyJump, where is the administrator's private key during the session to web?
hint: The session is end to end.

choices.text: Copied to jump for the length of the session, then deleted
choices.why: Nothing is copied; that was the old way's problem.

choices.text: On jump's agent, because AllowAgentForwarding hands it over
choices.why: The bastion sets AllowAgentForwarding no.

choices.text: Only on admin
choices.why: Right. jump carries an encrypted connection it cannot read.

choices.text: On web, which keeps a copy after the first login
choices.why: A server receives a signature, never the private key.

prompt: `ssh jump` prints `This account is currently not available.` Which line of the bastion's policy did that?

choices.text: PermitOpen web:22
choices.why: That limits where the bastion connects, not what runs on it.

choices.text: ForceCommand /usr/sbin/nologin
choices.why: Right. Every command asked for runs nologin instead.

choices.text: AllowAgentForwarding no
choices.why: That keeps the agent away from the bastion; it prints nothing.

choices.text: X11Forwarding no
choices.why: That is about graphical programs.

prompt: `ssh -J jump desk hostname` fails with `stdio forwarding failed`, though the key is valid. Why?

choices.text: desk's firewall refuses connections from jump
choices.why: No rule was written on desk; jump never tried.

choices.text: ProxyJump only works when the target is called web
choices.why: It works to any target the bastion is allowed to open.

choices.text: The key was rejected by jump, which ends the whole attempt
choices.why: The key was accepted; the forwarding request was refused.

choices.text: PermitOpen lists only web:22
choices.why: Right. The bastion refuses to open anything else.

prompt: On web, SSH_CONNECTION starts with 192.168.60.40 for a session typed on admin. What does that show?

choices.text: web sees jump, not admin, as the client
choices.why: Right, which is what lets web's firewall name jump alone.

choices.text: admin's address was rewritten by the switch on the way
choices.why: sw only bridges; jump opened the connection itself.

choices.text: The configuration entry was ignored and admin connected directly
choices.why: Directly, the address would be admin's, 192.168.60.30.

choices.text: The session is not encrypted between jump and web
choices.why: It is encrypted end to end; the address says nothing about that.

prompt: Why does web answer desk with `reject with tcp reset` instead of dropping silently?

choices.text: Because a dropped packet is still counted as accepted
choices.why: Drop and count work together; nothing is accepted.

choices.text: Inside the firm, a fast refusal saves the administrator a timeout
choices.why: Right. Toward the internet lesson 5 weighs the other choice.

choices.text: Because nftables cannot drop TCP packets
choices.why: It can; lesson 14 dropped port 53 on the switch.

choices.text: To tell desk which machine it should use instead
choices.why: A reset carries no such information.

prompt: web accepts SSH only from jump. Why does jump also accept SSH only from admin?

choices.text: Because jump has no fail2ban to protect it
choices.why: fail2ban runs on every machine of the lab.

choices.text: Because web would otherwise reject jump too
choices.why: web's rule names jump's address; what reaches jump does not change it.

choices.text: Otherwise a key stolen anywhere still reaches the bastion
choices.why: Right. The door is only one door if the way to it is narrow too.

choices.text: Because ProxyJump needs both ends on the same rule
choices.why: ProxyJump knows nothing about firewall rules.

prompt: Once every administrator uses the bastion, what does a rising counter on web's reject rule mean?

choices.text: That the bastion is overloaded
choices.why: Traffic through the bastion arrives from its address and is accepted.

choices.text: Somebody or something is trying the old way in
choices.why: Right. It is worth watching.

choices.text: That the certificate authority needs a new key
choices.why: Refused packets never reached the certificate check.

choices.text: That fail2ban has started banning administrators by mistake
choices.why: This counter belongs to the nftables rule, not to fail2ban.

prompt: What does an SSH user certificate add to a plain key?

choices.text: A longer key, which is harder to guess
choices.why: The key is the same; the signature and its fields are new.

choices.text: An authority's signature, a validity period and allowed account names
choices.why: Right: -s, -V and -n in the command.

choices.text: A password that protects the private key
choices.why: That is a passphrase, which a certificate does not need or give.

choices.text: Encryption of the session
choices.why: Every SSH session is encrypted, with or without a certificate.

prompt: The lab keeps the user CA's private key in ana's home on admin. What does the lesson say a real firm does?

choices.text: Keeps it on every server, so each can sign locally
choices.why: Then stealing any server would make anybody an administrator.

choices.text: Publishes it, since the servers need to check signatures
choices.why: Servers need the public half only.

choices.text: Keeps it on the bastion, which every session crosses
choices.why: The bastion faces every administrator; the signing key belongs further away.

choices.text: Keeps it offline, with signing logged
choices.why: Right: a hardware token or a dedicated signing service.

prompt: After `AuthorizedKeysFile none`, somebody appends a public key to /home/ana/.ssh/authorized_keys on web. What happens when they use it?

choices.text: It is refused: the file is no longer read
choices.why: Right. Only a certificate the authority signed gets in.

choices.text: It works until the next reload of sshd
choices.why: The setting is already loaded; the file is ignored from now on.

choices.text: It works, because the key belongs to ana, who has a certificate
choices.why: The certificate covers the key it was made for, not new ones.

choices.text: sshd stops, because the file contradicts the setting
choices.why: Nothing contradicts anything; the file is simply not consulted.

prompt: A certificate valid for one hour is stolen ten minutes after it was signed. What does the lesson name for that case?

choices.text: Waiting, because nothing else exists
choices.why: Revocation exists; it is just rarely needed.

choices.text: RevokedKeys in the server's configuration
choices.why: Right. With an hour's lifetime it is the exception.

choices.text: Removing the line from authorized_keys on every server
choices.why: There is no such line; the servers trust the authority.

choices.text: Signing a new certificate with the same identity, which replaces the stolen one
choices.why: A new certificate does not cancel the old one.

prompt: The certificate's list of account names it may log in as is printed by ssh-keygen -L under the heading ___.
hint: It is a word from the transcript.

prompt: Three administrators all log in to web as ana with certificates. What in the log tells them apart?

choices.text: The source address, which differs per person
choices.why: Every session comes from jump, 192.168.60.40.

choices.text: The key fingerprint, since each person has a different key
choices.why: Useful, but it names a key, not a person; the identity field is written for that.

choices.text: The certificate's ID, written at signing
choices.why: Right, matched to the authority's record of who asked.

choices.text: The port the session came from
choices.why: Ports are chosen at random by the client.

prompt: Which setting made web write the certificate's ID and authority into its log?

choices.text: TrustedUserCAKeys
choices.why: That names the authority to trust; it does not change the log.

choices.text: PasswordAuthentication no
choices.why: That refuses passwords.

choices.text: LogLevel VERBOSE
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: ForceCommand
choices.why: That was on jump, and it forces a command.

prompt: Why does the lesson treat a full session recording as sensitive data in itself?

choices.text: Because recordings are large and fill the disk
choices.why: Size is a cost, not a sensitivity.

choices.text: Because the law forbids recording administrators
choices.why: The lesson says to tell them, not that it is forbidden.

choices.text: Because a recording can be replayed to log in again
choices.why: A recording is not a credential; replaying it logs in nobody.

choices.text: It holds typed passwords and opened files
choices.why: Right, so it is kept where the recorded cannot alter it, and read only with a reason.

prompt: What is the gap a jump server leaves, which a privileged access workstation closes?

choices.text: The administrator's own workstation
choices.why: Right. A compromised admin uses the bastion as designed.

choices.text: The servers' firewalls, which the bastion cannot configure
choices.why: Those were written in this lesson and do their job.

choices.text: Certificates that expire, which a PAW renews automatically
choices.why: Expiry is the feature, not the gap.

choices.text: Encryption between jump and web, which a PAW adds
choices.why: That path is already encrypted end to end.

prompt: In the tier model, why must a tier 0 administrator never log in to a tier 2 workstation?

choices.text: Because tier 2 machines cannot run the tools tier 0 needs
choices.why: Tools are not the reason; exposure of credentials is.

choices.text: Because it would count against the workstation's licence
choices.why: Licensing has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: Whoever controls the workstation captures what they type
choices.why: Right: credentials only flow downwards.

choices.text: Because tier 2 sits on a separate network, out of tier 0's reach
choices.why: Reachability is not the rule; trust is.

prompt: Match each control with the weakness it removes.

pairs.left: web's firewall accepting SSH only from jump
pairs.right: a key stolen from desk still working on web
a departed employee's key working for years

pairs.left: PermitTTY no and ForceCommand on jump
pairs.right: a shell on the most sensitive machine
one local administrator password shared by every laptop

prompt: Put in order the steps this lesson takes, each one depending on the one before.
items: make jump a door with no shell
route admin's sessions to web through jump
make web accept SSH from jump only
make web trust the authority instead of key files
read the certificate identity in web's log

prompt: How many SSH connections does `ssh -J jump web` open from admin's side, counting the inner one?
hint: One to the bastion, one carried through it.

prompt: At the end of the lesson, which of these still gets a shell on web? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: admin with a valid certificate, through jump
choices.why: That is the one door.

choices.text: desk with ana's plain key, directly
choices.why: Refused by web's firewall, and the plain key no longer counts.

choices.text: admin with a certificate that expired an hour ago
choices.why: The transcript shows it refused.

choices.text: root at web's own console, through hostlab.sh
choices.why: Physical or console access is not SSH, and no rule here touches it.
